> Method, metrics and limitations are in the
> [02 · Late-Delivery Model report](02-late-delivery.qmd).

## Bottom line

The model ranks late risk better than a customer-state baseline, but the signal is
modest and the capacity curve is irregular. The riskiest 10% contains **1.97×** its
share of late orders; the riskiest 5% is *less* precise than the 10% slice. **This
is a research prototype, not a deployment-ready queue.**

## The finding

- Trained on **43,691 mature orders** purchased before January 2018 and tested on
  **32,150** purchased from April 2018, the selected logistic model reaches
  **ROC AUC 0.685** and **average precision 0.082** against a **4.42%** base rate.
- Flagging the **top 10% (3,215 orders)** captures **19.7% of all late orders**
  at **8.7% precision**, a **1.97× lift**. A customer-state baseline captures
  12.2% at the same capacity, 1.22× the base rate. At 5% capacity, precision is
  **7.7%** and recall 8.7%; at 20%, precision is 9.2% and recall 41.8%.
- **The earlier 2.35× lift was too high.** The previous training rule kept only
  orders already delivered by the test cutoff. That removed 3,852 orders with a
  **39.1% late rate** — the slow orders the model is meant to find. Training now
  stops three months before the cutoff, and the honest lift is smaller.
- **The model class is not settled.** Logistic regression won the rolling-origin
  comparison (mean AP 0.119 vs 0.108), while gradient boosting did slightly
  better on the final holdout (AP 0.087 vs 0.082; recall 21.8% vs 19.7%). A
  paired bootstrap puts the logistic-minus-boosting AP difference at **−0.0048
  (95% interval −0.0122 to +0.0036)**. The interval includes zero.
- **The score is not a probability.** Mean predicted risk is 4.26% against 4.42%
  observed, but the calibration slope is 0.82 and the intercept −0.47. The
  ranking is compressed; do not attach the percentage to an individual order.
- **Promise and geography do the work.** `promise_days`, customer state and seller
  state dominate. Basket value, freight, weight, payment and category add little.
- **The signal moves with the period.** Monthly AUC in the holdout ranges from
  0.60 to 0.79; rolling origins from 0.59 to 0.62.

## What it is allowed to see

Only information that exists when the order is placed: purchase timing, the
promised date, customer and seller state, order composition and payment terms.
Approval, carrier hand-off, delivery date, days late, review score and order
status are excluded by an explicit allow-list. Using arrival time would make the
model look excellent and be useless at the only moment it could help.

Training labels must also have matured before the cutoff. An order purchased in
March but delivered in May cannot teach a model deployed on 1 April, because its
outcome was not known yet. The training window therefore stops three months
before the test cutoff. A naive “purchase before April, keep delivered” rule
would instead select on delivery speed and remove the late tail.

## Recommendation

1. **Do not deploy this as a triage queue yet.** The lift is modest, the top 5%
   is less precise than the top 10%, and there is no cost model. Run a
   prospective pilot only if the operation can measure the late rate in reviewed
   versus unreviewed orders.
2. **Do not expose the score as a customer-facing probability.** If one is
   needed, recalibrate on recent delivered orders and re-check monthly.
3. **Keep the rolling evaluation and retrain as labels mature.** A production
   system would not freeze the training window at one date; it would retrain
   monthly and monitor the late rate, the promise distribution and the state mix.
4. **Keep Project 01's operational question first.** The model confirms that
   promise length and the seller–customer state pair carry the signal. It does
   not say that changing the promise causes a better outcome; the corridor
   question from Project 01 remains the causal one.

## What would change my mind

- **If a prospective pilot shows a stable lift at a capacity the team can
  actually staff**, the model becomes operationally interesting. The current
  evidence is retrospective.
- **If reviewed orders turn out to be late for reasons the model cannot see**
  (carrier allocation, warehouse backlog), the score is a proxy for the lane and
  the intervention should target the lane instead.
- **If a carrier or warehouse identifier becomes available**, it should be tested
  before any further feature engineering; it is the most likely missing cause.

---

*All figures above come from `projects/02-late-delivery/reports/model_metrics.json`
and are reproducible with `uv run python tasks.py train`. The 95% bootstrap
interval for top-decile precision is 7.7–9.6%, for recall 17.7–21.7%, and for
lift 1.77–2.17×.*
